title: Of whom does the “I” of Romans 7:14–25 speak?
summary: Romans 7:9 has the speaker say “I was alive without the law once”, and 7:14 says “I am carnal, sold under sin”, while 7:22 says “I delight in the law of God after the inward man”. The passage does not say whether “I” is Paul before, or after, he came to Christ, or every person, or Israel under the law, or another figure.
text: KJV Romans 7:9: “I was alive without the law once”. KJV Romans 7:14: “I am carnal, sold under sin”. Greek New Testament (Tischendorf, eighth edition) Romans 7:14: ἐγὼ δὲ σάρκινός εἰμι, πεπραμένος ὑπὸ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν [but I am fleshly, sold under sin]. KJV Romans 7:22: “I delight in the law of God after the inward man”. KJV Romans 7:25: “with the mind I myself serve the law of God; but with the flesh the law of sin”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/TISCH/45/7/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/TR/45/7/.
reasoning: The passage is written in the first person singular and in the present tense from 7:14, and it has the speaker both sold under sin (7:14) and delighting in the law of God (7:22). It does not name who is speaking or when. Different readings are held as possibilities only: Paul describing his own state before he believed, Paul describing his state as a believer, a figure standing for any person under the law, or a figure standing for Israel at Sinai. The text does not choose among them, and the verses before and after (7:5–6 and 8:1–2) are held in the passage’s own argument.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to Romans 7:7–25 and 8:1–2 as the context. The record does not say which reading is right and does not claim that no other passage of the Bible says more about the matter. The Greek quoted is Tischendorf’s eighth edition as served by bolls.life; the Textus Receptus text served prints σαρκικός where Tischendorf’s text prints σάρκινος, which this record does not treat as the question. The Greek New Testament wording is Tischendorf’s eighth edition as served by bolls.life (TISCH), compared with the Textus Receptus text served there (TR); neither is a critical apparatus.

title: Who is “him who hath subjected the same” to vanity in Romans 8:20?
summary: Romans 8:20 says that “the creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him who hath subjected the same in hope”. The verse does not say who “him” is, and does not say when the subjecting happened.
text: KJV Romans 8:20: “the creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him who hath subjected the same in hope”. Greek New Testament (Tischendorf, eighth edition) Romans 8:20: διὰ τὸν ὑποτάξαντα [on account of the one who subjected]. KJV Romans 8:21: “the creature itself also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption”. KJV Romans 8:22: “the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/TISCH/45/8/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/TR/45/8/.
reasoning: The verse has an agent in a participle (“him who hath subjected”) and does not name the agent. It also does not say what the agent did or when. Different readings are held as possibilities only: God, who subjected it as a judgment and in hope; Adam, through whose act the creation fell under a curse; or another agent. The text does not choose among them. The verse does give the purpose, “in hope”, and the following verses give the end, deliverance (8:21).
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to Romans 8:19–22. The record does not say which reading is right, does not say that any other passage of the Bible names the agent, and does not claim that no other passage says more. title: In what sense are Andronicus and Junia “of note among the apostles”?
summary: Romans 16:7 says “Salute Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen, and my fellow-prisoners, who are of note among the apostles, who also were in Christ before me”. The verse does not say whether they were themselves apostles or were well known to the apostles, and it says nothing else about who they were or when and where they were imprisoned.
text: KJV Romans 16:7: “my fellow-prisoners, who are of note among the apostles, who also were in Christ before me”. Greek New Testament (Tischendorf, eighth edition) Romans 16:7: ἐπίσημοι ἐν τοῖς ἀποστόλοις [notable among the apostles]. KJV Acts 14:14: “the apostles, Barnabas and Paul”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/TISCH/45/16/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/TR/45/16/.
reasoning: The Greek phrase “among the apostles” can be read as a statement about the two, that they are apostles and notable ones, or as a statement of how the apostles regard them. The verse supplies no list of apostles against which to test either. The word “apostle” is used elsewhere in the book of Acts of Barnabas and Paul (Acts 14:14) as well as of the twelve, so the word’s range in the book is wider than one group; that does not settle which reading Romans 16:7 takes. The text does not choose among the readings.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to Romans 16:7, with Acts 14:14 quoted only as another place where the word “apostles” is applied beyond the twelve. The record does not say which reading is right, does not claim that no other passage of the Bible says more, and does not rest on the gender or the form of the name Junia, which it does not examine.
